steps.title: Now listen to four more.
steps.sub: Two are strengths, one is a weakness, one is an achievement.

items.text: I can work quickly.
I’m good at interviewing people.
I find it hard to say no.
I won an award for best young sports journalist.

steps.title: Look at the weakness again.
steps.sub: I find it hard to say no. That means I sometimes have too many projects. But I’m working on that.
steps.prompt: Why does the candidate add “but I’m working on that”?
options: A weakness answer should say what you are doing about it.
To make the answer longer.
Because the interviewer asked for two weaknesses.
steps.answer: A weakness answer should say what you are doing about it.
steps.why: Name a real weakness, explain the effect, then say what you are doing about it. That is the whole formula.

steps.title: The four questions almost every interview asks
steps.html:
The questionHow to start your answer
What qualifications have you got?I’ve got a degree in … / I have a diploma in …
How much experience do you have?I’ve worked as a … for six years. I’m currently …
Why do you want to work for us?I enjoy my present job, but I’d like to …
What are your strengths?I’m good at …ing. / I can … when I need to.
And your weaknesses?I find it hard to … That means … But I’m working on that.
What’s your greatest achievement?Two years ago I won … / I was most proud of …
Do you have any questions?Yes, I do have a few actually …

Experience takes the Present Perfect with for or since: I’ve worked as a journalist for six years — the grammar of Lesson 34.

A finished job takes the Past Simple: I worked there for two years and then I wrote for a magazine.

Strengths use I’m good at + -ing or I can + base form. Never say I have a good interviewing.

“Do you have any questions?” is a real question. Answering No looks like you are not interested — always have two ready.

This lesson brings together the question forms of Lesson 1, the tenses of Lessons 17 and 34, and the purpose infinitive of Lesson 35.

DANIELLE MOREAU
Montreal · d.moreau@mail.com · +1 514 000 0000

PROFILE
Sports journalist with six years’ experience in print and online media. Currently writing for a national ice hockey magazine. Looking for a role covering a wider range of sports.

EXPERIENCE

Staff writer, Shoot ice hockey magazine · 2022–present
Interview players and coaches; write two features a week; manage the magazine’s social media.

Writer, Teen Sport magazine · 2020–2022
Wrote weekly reports on school and junior competitions.

Junior reporter, Laval Daily · 2018–2020
Covered local sport. First job after university.

EDUCATION
BA Journalism, University of Montreal · 2015–2018. Included print, radio, TV and online journalism.

ACHIEVEMENTS
Best Young Sports Journalist award, 2023.

SKILLS
Interviewing · fast, accurate writing under pressure · English and French.

steps.title: Write your own CV.
steps.sub: Use the six sections of the model. Real or invented — but consistent.
steps.html:
1. Plan (from the model): name and contact → profile in three lines → experience, newest first, with dates and what you did → education → achievements → skills → referees.
  • NAME · city · email · phone
  • PROFILE: … with … years’ experience in … Currently … Looking for …
  • EXPERIENCE: job title, place, dates — what you did
  • EDUCATION: qualification, place, dates
  • ACHIEVEMENTS: …
  • SKILLS: …
  • REFEREES: available on request
PROFILEEXPERIENCEEDUCATIONACHIEVEMENTSSKILLSREFEREESyears’ experience inCurrentlyLooking forawardrangeavailable on request
steps.modelHtml:
• I used all six sections.
  • My jobs are listed newest first, with dates.
  • Each job says what I actually did, not just the title.
  • My profile is three lines or fewer.
  • There are no complete sentences with I in the experience section — CVs use short phrases.
